similar_scenes.name: Funk industrial
similar_scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
similar_scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
similar_scenes.desc: Tras la caída de P-Funk, muchos ritmos nuevos vinieron de fuera: Kraftwerk, Art of Noise («Beat Box», «Close (to the Edit)»), Talking Heads (Stop Making Sense, con Bernie Worrell) y el «Genius of Love» de Tom Tom Club. Herbie Hancock pidió a su mánager Tony Meilandt unos temas de hip hop y con Bill Laswell y Grandmixer D.S.T. hizo «Rockit» (Future Shock, 1983): la cima del funk industrial nada más empezar. Laswell (Material, Time Zone con John Lydon, Manu Dibango, los Last Poets) dejó su sello de bajo grueso; sellos como Celluloid, On-U Sound, Tommy Boy o Def Jam sacaban ritmos ásperos de raspados metálicos y tensión de Guerra Fría. On-U Sound de Adrian Sherwood fichó a la sección rítmica de Sugarhill (Doug Wimbish, Skip McDonald, Keith LeBlanc): Tackhead, el «No Sell Out» con la voz de Malcolm X, «el P-Funk de los ochenta» según Pedro Bell.
similar_scenes.family: Hip hop, go-go y funk de los noventa

similar_scenes.name: Metal industrial
similar_scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
similar_scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
similar_scenes.desc: El cruce del thrash con la música industrial de baile: Godflesh, Fear Factory o Rammstein. En la frontera están Ministry y Nine Inch Nails, que quizá sean más bien música industrial metalizada.
similar_scenes.family: Cruces: rap, funk, industrial, grunge y nu metal

similar_scenes.name: Throbbing Gristle
similar_scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
similar_scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
similar_scenes.desc: Nacidos del grupo de performance COUM Transmissions (Fluxus, accionistas vieneses, sexo y fluidos corporales en galerías), Genesis P-Orridge, Cosey Fanni Tutti, Peter «Sleazy» Christopherson y Chris Carter giran hacia la cultura pop para desafiar a un público más amplio. El escándalo de Prostitution en el ICA (1976) los convierte en enemigos públicos. «Antimúsica»: sin batería, instrumentos tocados como un niño, el «Gristle-izer» (un sampler primitivo), infrasonidos, improvisación en directo y una «línea de montaje sonora». Su sello Industrial Records y el lema «Music from the Death Factory» bautizan un género. The Second Annual Report, el electro pop torcido de «United» y «Hot on the Heels of Love», D.o.A., 20 Jazz Funk Greats y Heathen Earth; coqueteos con la imaginería nazi, la pedofilia y el supervivencialismo militar de Monte Cazazza («Subhuman», «Discipline»). La «misión terminó» en 1981; P-Orridge funda Psychic TV.

similar_scenes.name: Música industrial
similar_scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
similar_scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
similar_scenes.desc: La progenie de Throbbing Gristle: espíritus afines (Cabaret Voltaire, Non, SPK, Z'ev) y una segunda ola innumerable de paisajes de ruido o metrónomo teutónico (Lustmord, Nocturnal Emissions, Death in June, Laibach, Skinny Puppy, Front 242, Merzbow). Whitehouse lleva el género al deleite descarado en el mal con la «power electronics»; Nurse with Wound (Steve Stapleton) prefiere el collage surrealista a lo Lautréamont y el krautrock. Excepciones rítmicas: Clock DVA (Thirst) y 23 Skidoo (Seven Songs, «Porno Bass»), que dejan entrar el funk negro, Fela Kuti y la world music.

similar_scenes.name: Industrial y acid punk de San Francisco
similar_scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
similar_scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
similar_scenes.desc: La tercera edad dorada de la bohemia de San Francisco: Factrix quería «llevar el teatro de la crueldad al rock» con instrumentos modificados (el Optigan tocado al revés), percusión africana programada y la guitarra lisérgica de Bond Bergland, «discípulos del feedback». Con Monte Cazazza y los robots de Mark Pauline (Survival Research Laboratories) montan espectáculos como Night of the Succubus (1981). Chrome, de Damon Edge y Helios Creed, inventa un «acid punk» o cyberpunk de guitarra corrosiva tras escuchar Never Mind the Bollocks: Alien Soundtracks, Half Machine Lip Moves. También Z'ev y Nervous Gender, documentados por Subterranean en Live at Target.

similar_scenes.name: Música industrial
similar_scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
similar_scenes.desc: El término lo usa por primera vez Monte Cazazza, pero su significado se define en Sheffield: Throbbing Gristle y Cabaret Voltaire usan el ruido de la fábrica como metáfora de la condición humana a finales del siglo XX. Throbbing Gristle (Second Annual Report, «música de la fábrica de la muerte»; 20 Jazz Funk Greats abre la puerta al industrial bailable y al synth-pop), Cabaret Voltaire, Clock DVA. Con los sellos independientes, la diversificación: Nurse With Wound, Zoviet France, This Heat, 23 Skidoo, Current 93 (y su folk apocalíptico), Hafler Trio, Coil, Psychic TV, Test Dept, Lustmord. Desde Australia, Foetus, el primer compositor «clásico» de la civilización punk (Hole, Nail, Thaw). En EE UU, Arcane Device y Controlled Bleeding.

similar_scenes.name: Metal industrial y post-industrial
similar_scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
similar_scenes.desc: Uno de los logros clave de finales de los ochenta: la fusión de música industrial con hard rock y heavy metal, iniciada por los suizos Young Gods (samples de guitarras metálicas) y KMFDM. Chicago la completa: Ministry de Al Jourgensen (The Land Of Rape And Honey, «Jesus Built My Hot Rod»), Revolting Cocks, Pigface de Martin Atkins y, de ahí, Nine Inch Nails de Trent Reznor, que cambia el destino del industrial (Pretty Hate Machine, The Downward Spiral). El post-industrial: Neurosis, Steel Pole Bath Tub, Cop Shoot Cop, Missing Foundation, Pain Teens, Godflesh de Justin Broadrick, y los proyectos de Jello Biafra (Lard, Tumor Circus).

similar_scenes.name: La segunda venida del industrial
similar_scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
similar_scenes.desc: En los noventa el estilo brutal de Nine Inch Nails lo invade todo en EE UU y el industrial se vuelve fenómeno de masas; el «aggro» de KMFDM es menos visible pero igual de ubicuo: Grotus, Filter, Stabbing Westward, Acumen, Skrew, Electric Hellfire Club, Society Burning, Gravity Kills y, lo más original, Girls Vs Boys (Venus Luxure No.1 Baby) y New Wet Kojak. La EBM internacional se vuelve más brutal (Leaether Strip, Suicide Commando, :Wumpscut:, Hocico, Mentallo & The Fixer). La «música de la fábrica de la muerte» sobrevive en los escultores de ruido: los neozelandeses Dead C (Harsh '70s Reality, «música imposible de escuchar»), Gate, Bruce Russell, Namanax, Illusion Of Safety, Maeror Tri, Towering Inferno (Kaddish). Y el «digital hardcore» de Atari Teenage Riot y Alec Empire.

similar_scenes.name: Industrial, EBM y The Final Cut
similar_scenes.book: Techno Rebels: The Renegades of Electronic Funk
similar_scenes.author: Dan Sicko
similar_scenes.desc: En 1989-1990 quien no escuchaba techno escuchaba industrial: Nitzer Ebb, Skinny Puppy, Front Line Assembly y los belgas Front 242 (Front by Front, 1988), con Chicago como centro americano (Ministry, Die Warzau, My Life with the Thrill Kill Kult, Wax Trax). Detroit tuvo su escena: Code Industry, el único grupo industrial enteramente afroamericano, y The Final Cut, de Jeff Mills y Tony Srock, banda de apoyo del grupo house True Faith (con Bridgett Grace) en Paragon, cuyo productor Jerry Capaldi acabó enfrentado a sus artistas y sembró desconfianza entre techno negro y blanco. Deep into the Cut (1990, Big Sex/Interfisch) cruzó EBM y techno; la última cita de Mills con ellos fue en el festival Atonal de Berlín. Srock los llevó hacia el rock (Consumed, Nettwerk, 1991).
similar_scenes.family: Raíces: Kraftwerk, electro, funk, italo y new wave

similar_scenes.name: Industrial
similar_scenes.book: Loops 1 y 2. Una historia de la música electrónica
similar_scenes.author: Javier Blánquez (ed.)
similar_scenes.desc: Subvierte la vanguardia apropiándose del ruido; el ruido se vuelve fuente de terror, catarsis, provocación y placer.

similar_scenes.name: Rhythm & noise
similar_scenes.book: Loops 1 y 2. Una historia de la música electrónica
similar_scenes.author: Javier Blánquez (ed.)
similar_scenes.desc: Corriente lateral del industrial que, al calor del techno, forma una escena violenta y seca de baile experimental post-rave.

similar_scenes.name: Esoterismo post-industrial
similar_scenes.book: Loops 1 y 2. Una historia de la música electrónica
similar_scenes.author: Javier Blánquez (ed.)
similar_scenes.desc: Francotiradores inclasificables adoptados por la escena industrial que hicieron del ruido algo onírico y surreal: Coil (magia crowleyana, fantasías homoeróticas, «una mezcla de electricidad y drogas»), Psychic TV y su secta Thee Temple ov Psychick Youth, Nurse With Wound (krautrock + surrealismo), Current 93 (cut-up y folk) y el catalán Jordi Valls con Vagina Dentata Organ.

similar_scenes.name: Rock industrial
similar_scenes.book: Loops 1 y 2. Una historia de la música electrónica
similar_scenes.author: Javier Blánquez (ed.)
similar_scenes.desc: Hoy «industrial» es a menudo sinónimo de ritmos hormigonados y looks apocalípticos que cotizan al alza en las listas gracias a Nine Inch Nails o Ministry.

similar_scenes.name: Techno oscuro / post-industrial
similar_scenes.book: Loops 1 y 2. Una historia de la música electrónica
similar_scenes.author: Javier Blánquez (ed.)
similar_scenes.desc: Tras el minimal, el techno vuelve a la fuerza y la oscuridad pero a menor tempo (120-130 bpm), con espacio para matices de dub, dubstep, IDM e industrial: refugio de la música de club intelectualizada frente a la EDM. Sandwell District (Regis, Function, Female, Silent Servant), Surgeon, el techno hipnótico de Donato Dozzy o Mike Parker y sellos como Semántica.

podcast.title: Early Characteristics (Pre-1982)
podcast.body: Before about 1982, industrial music was characterized by the "cold, clanging and banging" sounds pioneered by bands like Throbbing Gristle and Einstürzende Neubauten. "Before about 1982, industrial music was the domain of bands like Throbbing Crystal and I was ending Noe Bowden with their cold, clanging and banging."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Increased Guitar Use (By 1987)
podcast.body: By 1987, guitars became much more commonly used in industrial music, especially by North American groups such as Skinny Puppy and Ministry, indicating a shift in the genre's sonic palette. "By 1987, it was very clear that things were changing rapidly on the industrial scene. Thanks to groups like Skinny Puppy and Ministry, guitars were being used a lot more, especially by North American industrial groups."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolution from 1988 to Present
podcast.body: The period from 1988 onwards has been a significant time for industrial music fans, with the genre evolving from its primitive clanging and banging into a sophisticated amalgam of metal, distortion, percussion, samplers, and synthesizers. While its widespread popularity from the 1990s has diminished, it remains a distinct and hard-edged musical form. "It's evolved from the primitive clang and banging into something very sophisticated. It's an amalgam of metal, distortion, percussion, samplers, and synthesizers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: David Bowie's Incorporation (1997)
podcast.body: Industrial music was one of the new dance genres that David Bowie became interested in and incorporated into his 1997 album, *Earthling*. This was seen by some as Bowie giving his official recognition to the genre. "He'd become interested in various new genres of dance music, including industrial, techno, jungle, and drum and bass."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: US Military Lawsuit (2014)
podcast.body: Canadian industrial pioneer Skinny Puppy sued the US military for $666,000 in 2014 after discovering their music was used without permission for "enhanced interrogation" on prisoners at Guantanamo Bay, as revealed by a former guard. "In 2014, Canadian industrial pioneer Skinny Puppy sued the US military for using their music on prisoners."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Terrorist Sounds"
podcast.body: This genre emerged from "terrorist sounds" and noise, representing an extreme anti-rock approach to destroying music, often associated with pioneers like Throbbing Gristle. "directamente los terroristas sonidos que acabaron creando un género basaron el ruido, la música industrial."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: La traición que salvó al punk. PiL

podcast.title: 80s Alt-Rock Radio Inclusion
podcast.body: Industrial music was among the diverse genres featured on alt-rock radio playlists in the 1980s, demonstrating the broad range of music played before the rise of grunge.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Aggressive Turn in North America (Early 1990s)
podcast.body: In North America, music had turned aggressive in some quarters, including industrial music, indicating early shifts. "And dust-trimon music and hardcore, for example."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Basic Enduring Sound
podcast.body: Industrial music is listed as one of the basic and enduring sounds that will never go away, but is continuously challenged by new genres. "The basic sounds are still with us. Rock, alternative, indie, Goth, industrial, metal, synth-based music, ska, reggae, and so on. They're never going to go away."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 3: The New Genres

podcast.title: Breakthrough in Early 90s
podcast.body: A "strange thing happened at the beginning of the 90s" when a number of industrial-minded groups broke through into the mainstream, some even before Grunge, possibly due to "anxiety brought on by the first Gulf War," the "intense recession," or "never-ending Republican rule in the US." "But then a strange thing happened at the beginning of the 90s. Maybe it was the anxiety brought on by the first Gulf War. Maybe it was the intense recession. Maybe it was the never-ending Republican rule in the US."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: British Invention and Rapid Spread
podcast.body: Industrial music was a British invention that emerged quickly following the punk movement. Alongside Goth, Technopop, and Modern Skah, it experienced rapid dissemination and often a brief existence, influenced by the intense cultural churn within the British Isles. "There was Goth and Tecdopop and Industrial, Modern Skah, which were all basically British inventions."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Brutal and Heavy Programming
podcast.body: The inherent ability of keyboards and drum machines to be programmed to create brutal and heavy sounds inevitably led some musicians to explore this direction, cementing its roots in electronic music. "Because keyboards and drum machines could be programmed to sound so brutal and heavy, it was inevitable that some musicians would take this root."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Roots of New Wave through Techno-Pop

podcast.title: Challenging Guitar's Role
podcast.body: A key goal for these artists was to demonstrate that the electric guitar was not necessary for music, or at the very least, could be utilized in ways other than a conventional rock instrument. "The goal by these artists and others was to show that the electric guitar wasn't necessary, or at the very least, could be something other than a conventional rock instrument."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Characteristics
podcast.body: Industrial music is characterized by guitars, synthesizers, and driving beats, with acts like Nine Inch Nails, Marilyn Manson, and Ministry being prominent examples. "Industrial music is another option. guitars, synthesizers, and driving beats from acts like nine-inch nails in Maryland, Manson, and ministry."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Close Cousin to Goth
podcast.body: Industrial music is considered a "close cousin" to Goth, sharing characteristics like darkness, introspection, and a dominant black fashion color. "A close cousin of Goth is industrial music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Continued Remixing in Grunge Era
podcast.body: While rock-based remixes declined with the advent of grunge, remixing continued to be a practice for industrial groups, along with electronic outfits and a few other genres. "Oh, it was still done for industrial groups, electronic outfits and a few others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Creation by Cabaret Voltaire
podcast.body: Industrial Music, described as a heavy form of electronic music, was developed with contributions from bands like Cabaret Voltaire, who were part of the Factory Records roster. "Cabaret Voltaire, who helped create the heavy form of electronic music called Industrial Music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 2

podcast.title: Cultural Context
podcast.body: Industrial music thrived in "dark clubs" with loud music and sometimes violent dancing, and its practitioners and fans collectively conveyed a message to "wake up, sheeple, question authority, think for yourselves, and be honest about the pain you feel." "It thrived in dark clubs, where the music was loud and the dancing was sometimes violent. Its practitioners and fans were collectively shouting, wake up, sheeple, question authority, think for yourselves, and be honest about the pain you feel."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: David Bowie's Importance
podcast.body: David Bowie was considered very important to fans of industrial music, particularly those who admired Nine Inch Nails. His experimental and electronic soundscapes, especially during his Berlin period, laid crucial groundwork that resonated with and influenced the industrial genre. "And if you loved industrial music, Bowie was very important to you, especially if you were a fan of 9-inch nails."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: David Bowie's Importance to Industrial Fans
podcast.body: David Bowie was very important to fans of industrial music, particularly those who admired Nine Inch Nails, reflecting his broad influence across genres. "And if you loved industrial music, Bowie was very important to you."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Discovery by Generation X
podcast.body: Generation X discovered Industrial music, which had existed outside the mainstream for years. "JNX discovered different flavors of Goth, an industrial, and electronic music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Industrial as Pre-Post Rock
podcast.body: Early industrial music, exemplified by groups like Britain's Throbbing Gristle and Germany's Einstürzende Neubauten, is considered to align with post-rock criteria through its experimental and unconventional use of instruments, particularly the electric guitar. "We could include early industrial music. Go back and listen to some of their first recordings by groups such as Britain's Throbbing Gristle and Germany's Einstein-Dé Noybaden."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Emergence as Enduring Post-Punk Subset
podcast.body: Industrial music emerged as a unique strand that survived the post-punk explosion of the late 1970s and early 1980s, becoming one of the most enduring subsets of alternative music. It budded off from Technopop. "This episode is about one such strand that survived the post-punk explosion of the late 1970s in early 80s. We call it industrial music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Esplendor Geométrico's Classification
podcast.body: Esplendor Geométrico, with their harsh, hypnotic, and noise-focused electronic music, were categorized within the industrial genre. Their unique sound resonated particularly well in noise-interested cultures outside Spain. "siendo engolovados dentro del género industrial."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: La España Siniestra ｜ La edad de oro del Postpunk y el Dark wave

podcast.title: Foundation in Technopop's First Wave
podcast.body: The cold, robotic sound of Technopop's first wave (1977-mid 1980) formed the fundamental basis for what would later be recognized as industrial music. "Songs like this formed the very basic foundations of what we would later call industrial music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Roots of New Wave through Techno-Pop

podcast.title: Foundations from Performance Art
podcast.body: The ideas and tenets demonstrated by harsh performance art bands like Throbbing Gristle began to lay the groundwork for what would later be recognized as industrial music. "These tenants and ideas began to lay the foundations of what we later call industrial music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fringe Existence
podcast.body: For a long time, industrial music "lived on the fringes of the Alt Rock universe," deemed "too heavy, too angry, too aggressive, too harsh, too distorted, too abrasive and just generally too intense for prime time." "For the longest time, industrial lived on the fringes of the Alt Rock universe. It was just too heavy, too angry, too aggressive, too harsh, too distorted, too abrasive and just generally too intense for prime time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Future Exploration of Post-Punk
podcast.body: Industrial music is described as one of the most intense, hard, and heavy forms of alternative music that emerged directly from the stratifications of punk, new wave, and Technopop, indicating its foundational ties to these earlier electronic and rebellious genres. "It's one of the most intense, hard, and heavy forms of alternative music known to humankind. We call it industrial."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Goth Crossover
podcast.body: Bands can cross a line from Goth into industrial when their sound reaches a certain "intensity and extremeness." "The sound reached a certain intensity and extremeness where they crossed that line from Goth into industrial."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Goth-tinged Genre
podcast.body: Industrial falls into the category of "Goth-tinged genres." "Industrial falls into this category."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hard and Heavy Sound
podcast.body: The primary difference between Industrial and Goth is Industrial's "very, very hard and very, very heavy" sound. "The main difference is that this music is very, very hard and very, very heavy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Industrial Music Overview (Early 1990s)
podcast.body: This genre was embraced by the "Lala Pulosa generation" in the US during the early 1990s, coexisting with grunge and hip hop. "They got into industrial music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Industrial Music – Throbbing Gristle Founded It; "Industrial Music for Industrial People"; Ministry and NIN Biggest Sellers
podcast.body: Industrial music's roots go back to the 1970s with Throbbing Gristle, who founded a label called Industrial Records with the motto "Industrial Music for Industrial People." The sound moved to Europe first, then was imported into the US in the early 1980s via a Chicago label named Wax Tracks, where it caught on with the corner of the alternative crowd seeking something powerful, angry, and brutal. Industrial fragmented into body music, power electronics, Japanoise (some of the most extreme music ever made), power noise, industrial metal, martial industrial, witch house, dark ambient, industrial hip-hop, and industrial techno. The two best-selling industrial bands are Ministry (which started as a synth-pop band) and Nine Inch Nails, whose Trent Reznor has done more than anyone to bring industrial music to the masses. "The two best-selling industrial bands of all time are Ministry, which started out as its fashion mode like synth band, and Nineteen Snails, headed up by Trent Resner."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence from Joy Division
podcast.body: The sound and style of Joy Division are credited with contributing significantly to the development of industrial music. "Their sound and style contributed to everything from the development of Goth to industrial music to Emo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Influence of Public Image Limited
podcast.body: Public Image Limited had a profound effect on the industrial music genre, with artists like Nine Inch Nails acknowledging their importance. "He hung out with some funk musicians, and eventually pulled together a band that ended up having a profound effect on several genres of music, including industrial and punk funk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 2

podcast.title: Key Bands
podcast.body: Throbbing Gristle and Coil are cited as two bands "very important to the industrial music scene" and were favorites of Trent Reznor. "Two bands very important to the industrial music scene and two favorites of Trent."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Kraftwerk's Foundational Impact
podcast.body: The question is posed whether industrial music would exist or be the same without Kraftwerk, highlighting their fundamental impact on the genre. "¿sin ellos existirían el tecno, el industrial o el Simpop?"

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Por qué KRAFTWERK es la banda más influyente de la historia?

podcast.title: Mid-1980s Redefinition
podcast.body: By the mid-1980s, industrial music underwent a redefinition. With Throbbing Gristle broken up and Einstürzende Neubauten incorporating chord changes, a new synthesis emerged. This new style combined the "factory sounds" of the original movement with aggressive Technopop elements, resulting in music that was loud, harsh, angry, dark, distorted, but also danceable. "But by the mid-1980s, there had been a change. Throbbing Crystal had broken up, Noe Bowden had discovered to use chord changes, and a new synthesis of styles was developing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Niche Sound and Indie Label Role
podcast.body: Industrial music was considered too heavy for most people, making it a niche sound that major labels typically avoided. This demand was subsequently filled by specialist indie labels such as Network Records of Vancouver and Wax Trax of Chicago. "This stuff is way too heavy for most people, making it, let's face in a real niche sound. Or at least it was for a while anyway. So that meant that major label stayed away."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 3

podcast.title: Off-shoot of Technopop
podcast.body: Industrial music is described as a "heavy off-shoot" of Technopop, which in turn emerged from New Wave following the punk rock era. This highlights its lineage as a more intense, darker branch of electronic and alternative music. "we've discussed the rise of new wave, the subset known as Tecno Pop, and its heavy off-shoot industrial music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origins and Influence
podcast.body: Industrial music, particularly the "rage and fury" found in bands like Ministry, Front 242, and Skinny Puppy, significantly influenced Trent Reznor's shift from techno-pop. This genre's aesthetic was pivotal in shaping the harder, more sinister sound that defined Nine Inch Nails. "He found that he really liked the rage and fury of bands like Ministry and Front242 and Canada's Skinny Puppy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Deep Dark Secrets of Nine Inch Nails

podcast.title: Popularity (Mid-90s)
podcast.body: Industrial music became popular in the early to mid-1990s, with groups like Nine Inch Nails and Ministry leading the way. "Industrial music was hot thanks to groups like Nine Inge Nails and Ministry."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Possible Influence of Glam Rock
podcast.body: It is suggested that industrial music may also owe its existence to the influence of glam rock. "You might even want to say the same thing about industrial music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Post-Punk Invention
podcast.body: Industrial music was another post-punk invention with roots in the "late 1970s," characterized by its reliance on electronics, often incorporating big guitars and live drums. "Take industrial music, for example. This was another post-punk invention with roots in the late 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Punk Subgenre
podcast.body: Industrial music, in a form of alternative dance, branched out from Technopop as one of the subgenres emerging from the post-punk era. "From that butted industrial music in a form of alternative dance"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Punk Subgenre
podcast.body: Industrial music is recognized as one of the major post-punk genres from the late 1970s and early 1980s, and is noted as a genre that is "still with us today." "There was new wave, techno pop, and all its subsets, industrial music, goth, and a revival of scot."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 7: All the rest

podcast.title: Production Spike in Early 1990s
podcast.body: The early 1990s experienced a "spike in the production of industrial music," suggesting an increase in its creation and popularity during that time. "there was a spike in the production of industrial music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Prolific Album Output
podcast.body: British industrial bands, notably Psychic TV, have demonstrated periods of extremely high productivity, releasing a remarkable number of albums in very short timeframes, even if some of the recordings were live and of varying quality. "The British industrial outfit called Psychic TV with Stranger Affair from their live and Paris album from 1986. That's part of their record-breaking run of releasing the most albums in the shortest period of time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Book of World Records Version 1.0 - Part 1

podcast.title: Retreat to Margins
podcast.body: Industrial music is still present today, but it has "again retreated to the margins," awaiting a future time when society might once more require "really, really angry music." "Industrial is still a thing. It's out there. But it's again retreated to the margins, awaiting a time when we once again need really, really angry music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Simultaneous Evolution with Goth
podcast.body: Goth and Industrial music have evolved simultaneously for years, with an "unspoken division of labor in terms of intensity." "Goth and Industrial have been evolving simultaneously for years now."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sound Characteristics
podcast.body: Industrial music is characterized as "hard and fast and heavy and distorted and angry." It relies on guitars and "sharp keyboard sounds of techno over ultra heavy beats." "While industrial is hard and fast and heavy and distorted and angry, Goth can be softer and slower and here's that word again, introspective."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Witchhouse Influence
podcast.body: Industrial music influenced Witchhouse, contributing elements like noisiness and an experimental, provocative spirit to the genre's sound. "del industrial, como el ruidismo y suspirito experimental y provocador..."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Witch House: Cuando internet inventó su género maldito

podcast.title: Yamaha DX7 Prominence in 1980s
podcast.body: The Yamaha DX7 synthesizer and its FM synthesis technology significantly shaped the sound of industrial music in the 1980s. The instrument's ubiquity meant its sounds were integrated into tracks across various genres, including industrial music, becoming a defining sonic characteristic of the era. "The DX7 and its FM synthesis technology really did become the sound of the 80s, no matter what the genre, including industrial music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Music Questions People Almost Never Ask
